title: Real water, better light and more wildlife
lede: The water is now clear enough to see stones and fish through it, the light comes from a sun that throws long shadows and lets mountains darken the valleys at dawn and dusk, the ground and forests carry far more detail, and fourteen new kinds of animals and birds live around you. Quality presets, dynamic resolution and an automatic step-down keep the frame rate up on older phones.

sections.title: Water you can see into
sections.html:
The old surface was a coloured sheet that hid everything under it. Now the surface only adds what really sits on water: reflections of the surroundings, glints from the sun and moon, and foam. Everything below it (the bed, the stones, the fish, a wading moose) is lit through the water by the objects themselves, with light absorbed along the bent path it takes through the water.

  • Colour by depth and kind of water. Shallow gravel stays clear; deeper pools turn green-blue in the river, tea-green in Moose Lake, milky turquoise in Glacier Lake (the upper river carries some of that silt) and blue-green at sea.
  • Caustics. Bright rippling light lines on the bottom in sunlight, fading with depth.
  • Real reflections. A small cube map of the sky, mountains, terrain and forests is captured from the water surface near you, one face per frame, so the far bank, peaks, sunsets, the moon and the northern lights all reflect, lit by the same sun and sky as everything else.
  • Moving water. Waves come from a small texture animated every frame with deep-water wave physics (long waves travel faster). The river flows along its course, rapids get rougher and whiter, lakes show calm and wind-ruffled patches, and a thin line of foam laps at the shore.
  • Wet ground. Stones and banks darken just above the waterline, and the pebble pattern on the river bed sways with the waves above it, like refraction.

sections.title: Fish you can spot
sections.html:
• Small schools hold in the current at the fishing hotspots and in nearby pools, noses upstream in the river and cruising in the lakes. Their species come from the same list the bites use, so a school of red sockeye means a sockeye can bite there.
  • They scatter when your float lands on them and drift back a moment later.
  • The fish that takes the bait is the real model: you watch it swim in under the float, nibble and turn away with the bait, and during the fight it runs and rolls under the surface at the end of your line.
  • During a salmon run the river fills with red sockeye.

figs.caption: A school of red sockeye holding in the river
The hooked pink salmon under the surface at the end of the line

sections.title: Better light
sections.html:
• Shadows much further out. The sun now casts two shadow layers fitted to what you see: sharp shadows up close and tree shadows out to about 250 metres (190 on Medium), where before they stopped at 70 metres.
  • Mountain shadows. A map on the graphics processor works out where the sun clears the mountains, refreshed a strip at a time as the sun moves, so valleys fall into shade at dawn and dusk while the peaks still glow.
  • Sky occlusion. Gullies, the foot of cliffs and the forest floor get less light from the sky, which gives the land depth.
  • Haze that matches the sky. The air thins with altitude and takes the colour of the sky in each direction, warm toward the sun, so distant ranges melt into the horizon instead of ending against a flat fog colour.
  • Leaves glow when the sun is behind them, and grass now falls into the shade of trees and mountains.
  • Neutral tone mapping for truer, clearer colours than before.

sections.title: More detail everywhere you look
sections.html:
• Ground by surface: rounded pebbles on gravel bars and river beds, layered and cracked rock on cliffs, ripples in sand and snow, needles and moss on the forest floor, all with bump lighting that catches the sun.
  • Trees: a new close-up spruce with drooping, ragged branch whorls and a closed underside, and a birch with forked limbs and a fuller crown, with the old models kept for the middle distance.
  • New plants: willow and alder thickets along the water, ferns under the trees, fireweed stands in the meadows and patches of lupine along roads and banks.
  • Dead wood: fallen logs with root plates, stumps, and bleached driftwood on gravel bars and beaches.
  • Boulders with rock texture and moss and lichen on their tops.
  • Grass: each blade is now two segments that stand up at the base and arch outward to a point, thinner than before and five to a tuft, with every blade its own shade from lush green to dry straw. Far from you the blades widen a little so they do not flicker.

Each has its own low-poly model and animation, and the calls are synthesised like the rest of the sound.

sections.title: Built to hold 60 frames per second
sections.html:
The target is a steady 60 frames per second on iPhone and iPad, where the game starts on the Medium preset. The new effects were built around what phones do cheaply:

  • Work spread over frames. The reflection cube renders one of its five useful faces per frame at 128 pixels (256 on High). The mountain-shadow map refreshes one strip of sixteen per frame. The wave texture is 256 pixels square.
  • Cheap stand-ins where detail cannot be seen. Reflections draw trees with their simplest model and a coarse, chunked copy of the terrain. That cut the triangles drawn for a reflection face at the landing from about 205 000 to about 96 000.
  • Fewer draw calls. Static buildings, docks and bridges are merged by material into one mesh per 160-metre cell (45 shadow-casting meshes became 27). Every animal species, every plant type and the fish are one instanced draw each.
  • Levels of detail. The detailed spruce and birch appear only within about 55 metres; ferns within 55 m and flowers within 70 to 85 m. All of these distances shrink on the lower presets.
  • Shaders compiled at startup, including the fish, so the first bite or the first bear does not stutter.
  • No shader switching from frame to frame. The reflection cube draws its own copies of the sky, terrain and tree materials and sees the same lights as the main view, and instanced shadow casters have their own depth materials. Before this fix the renderer looked up a different shader variant 38 times in every frame at Hotrod Landing; now it looks up none, which saves processor time and memory churn on phones.

Safeguards while you play

  • Dynamic resolution lowers the pixel density in steps when frames take longer than 1/40 of a second and raises it again when there is room.
  • Automatic step-down (new). If frames are still slow at the lowest resolution for three checks in a row, the game moves to the next lower preset and says so. Settings has an Adjust graphics automatically switch to turn this off.
  • Frame rate readout (new). Settings › Show frame rate puts the frames per second, the preset and the resolution under the clock (amber below 50, red below 35), so you can check it on your own device.

Rendering cost per view

Draw calls and triangles per frame, including the shadow passes and the reflection face, measured at 960 × 540 with the scripted views in tools/scenarios/perf-views.json. The same views before the update are the baseline.

ViewBefore: callsBefore: trianglesHigh: callsHigh: trianglesMedium: callsMedium: triangles

These counts come from a software renderer on the build machine, because no iPhone or iPad was available to measure on. Its frame times say nothing about a phone, so they are left out. The counts show how much more work each frame asks for; the actual frame rate still has to be read on a device with the readout above.

sections.title: What would change this conclusion
sections.html:
• A real device below 60 frames per second on Medium in the heaviest views (deep forest, Bear Falls, Hotrod Landing). The first levers are the Medium shadow distance and map size, the close-up tree distance, and fern and flower density. The automatic step-down already reacts in play, but it drops the whole preset.
  • A device without half-float render targets. The reflection cube then falls back to 8-bit colour, so bright sky and sun glints in reflections clip and look flatter. Every iPhone and iPad that runs the current iOS should support half floats, but this was not checked on hardware.
  • Heat on long sessions. Phones slow down when they get warm. If the readout sinks after twenty minutes of play, Low is the right preset for that device.
  • First launch. Compiling the larger shaders at startup takes longer than before, which lengthens the loading screen on older devices.

footer: Built on the claude/ruben-hotrod-fishing branch. The design follows well-known techniques: Snell's law for the bent path through the water, Schlick's approximation for the share of light the surface reflects, deep-water dispersion for the waves, caustics for the light lines on the bed, cascaded shadow maps for the sun shadows, and the Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapper as built into three.js. The build machine's network policy blocks these sites, so the links were written from knowledge and not opened from there.
